name: Femi Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo at Hollow Creek, the underground nickel mine on the old highway. A jumbo is a drill rig with two long arms, and I drill the face of a new tunnel, about sixty holes in a pattern, so the charge-up crew can blast it and we push the tunnel forward another four metres. Most of the day is lining up the booms and listening to the rock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real work, the same work my father did. You can see what you've done at the end of a shift. What wears me out is the money, honestly. I'm getting married next autumn to Ruth, who works at the bank in town, and we've just paid the deposit on the church hall, so we've got about two weeks of savings and a lot of plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it anyway. A computer can't drill a face. I'd say it at church, at the pub, and to my father, who'd agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my problem. The nickel price is my problem. Two mines near here closed last year when the price fell, and Hollow Creek cut overtime. My grandfather and my father both went underground at Hollow Creek, and I'd like to be the third, not the last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and take every shift they offered. I'd ask Ruth if we could make the wedding smaller, maybe the church hall but no band. And I'd ask my uncle about weekend work on his fencing jobs to build some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but used to it. Mining's always been up and down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the overtime cut hit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It took about three hundred a fortnight off my pay. That was our wedding saving, basically. Ruth's been very good about it, but I could tell she was disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use one of these AI tools, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've never needed one and I don't trust them. My father wrote his shift notes by hand and so do I.

say: I'd say a computer **can't drill a face**, so I never believed the hype.
I'd say it at **church** and to my father, who'd agree.
think: The **nickel price**, not AI, is my real problem.
Two nearby mines **closed last year**, and overtime has already been cut.
do: Keep **drilling** and take every shift offered.
Make the **wedding smaller** with no band.
Do weekend work on his uncle's **fencing jobs**.
feel: Worried but **used to it**, since mining has always gone up and down.
S0.quote: My grandfather and my father both went underground at Hollow Creek, and I'd like to be the third, not the last.
fieldNote: Femi is a **third-generation miner**, and pride runs through every answer.
Nickel price cuts already took **three hundred a fortnight** of wedding savings.
He won't touch **AI tools** and writes shift notes by hand.

steps.text: Take every jumbo shift offered at Hollow Creek
Cut the band and keep a smaller wedding in the church hall
Work weekends on his uncle's fencing jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see. People have been predicting the end of mining my whole life. I'd tell the young blokes to work hard and they'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about Ruth more than me. My fiancée Ruth answers customers at the bank all day, so in this picture her job is in more trouble than my drill is. Robots underground are slower to come, and I'd want to keep it that way as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and say no to any new screens or systems unless the company forced me. I'd encourage Ruth to look at jobs where people need a person, like the school office or the clinic. And we'd cut the honeymoon to a long weekend at the coast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit protective of Ruth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Ruth's hours were cut, how would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd live with my parents for a year after the wedding. My mother would be thrilled and I'd be less thrilled. But that's what family's for, not the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say no to new systems. What if the company made it part of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn it, slowly and grumbling. I'm stubborn, not stupid. I'd just be the last one to say yes.

say: I'd say **let's see**, because people have predicted mining's end for years.
I'd tell young miners to **work hard** and they'd be fine.
think: My fiancée's **bank job** is in more trouble than my drill.
**Robots underground** come slowly, and I'd keep it that way.
do: Refuse new **screens and systems** unless the company forces it.
Encourage Ruth to look at the **school office** or clinic.
Cut the **honeymoon** to a long weekend.
S1.quote: My fiancée Ruth answers customers at the bank all day, so in this picture her job is in more trouble than my drill is.
fieldNote: Femi sees thinking AI hit the **household** through Ruth's bank job first.
His fallback is **family**, living with his parents, never government help.
He calls himself **stubborn, not stupid**, and would learn if forced.

steps.text: Keep drilling and refuse optional new systems
Help Ruth apply for the school office or clinic
Live with his parents for a year after the wedding
Cut the honeymoon to a long weekend at the coast

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when people in cities who've never worked a day underground get to decide everything. I'd say working men need a say. I'd say it at church and at the pub, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be very scared. The planning and the office side go in 2028, so Ruth's bank job is gone first, and then robots come for the jumbo around 2031. I've paid the deposit on the church hall for the wedding, and I'd be paying it off with a job that's got three years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth if we should push the wedding back a year, which would break my heart. I'd take every shift going and save it all. I'd ask my father and the men at church who know someone in a trade that robots won't touch for a while, maybe plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. Like the floor of the tunnel's dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Plumbing is hands-on work too. Why plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every house has pipes, and every house is different. I don't know if a robot can crawl under a hundred-year-old house. Maybe it can by then. I'd still rather try that than sit around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, then the church. Pastor Daniel has found work for men before. I wouldn't go to the government unless there was nothing else.

say: I'd say **city people** who've never worked underground decide everything.
I'd say **working men** need a say, at church and at the pub.
think: Ruth's **bank job** goes in 2028, then my jumbo around 2031.
I'd be paying off the **wedding deposit** with a job that has three years left.
do: Ask Ruth about **delaying the wedding** a year.
Take **every shift** and save it all.
Ask his father and church about a **plumbing** apprenticeship.
feel: **Sick** to his stomach, like the tunnel floor dropping.
S2.quote: I've paid the deposit on the church hall for the wedding, and I'd be paying it off with a job that's got three years left.
fieldNote: Femi blames **city decision-makers**, not companies or workers.
Delaying the **wedding** would hurt him more than the job loss.
He'd turn to his father and **Pastor Daniel** before any government help.

steps.text: Push the wedding back by a year
Take every extra shift and save all of it
Find a plumbing apprenticeship through church contacts
Ask his father and Pastor Daniel for job leads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had warning, so there's no excuse. I'd want the company to run apprenticeships for miners, like they used to in my grandfather's day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still hate it, but I'd have a chance. Ruth's bank job goes by 2031, and the robots come underground around 2034. Five years is enough warning to be ashamed if I did nothing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned, small. I'd keep drilling and start asking about a plumbing apprenticeship within the first year, even if I only start in year two. And I'd save, properly, for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. But I'd feel like a man with a job to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You haven't mentioned using AI at all. Would you need to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little, for the apprenticeship paperwork. I'd ask Ruth to help me. I'd still not use it for anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably retrain too, maybe as a teacher's aide. She's quicker with change than me. We'd be two people learning at once, which is hard, but we'd manage.

say: I'd say we've **had warning**, so there's no excuse.
I'd want the company to run **apprenticeships** for miners again.
think: Ruth's **bank job** goes by 2031, and robots reach underground around 2034.
Doing nothing with **five years** would shame me.
do: Go ahead with a **small wedding** as planned.
Ask about a **plumbing apprenticeship** in the first year.
feel: Heavy, but with **a job to do**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough warning to be ashamed if I did nothing with it.
fieldNote: With five years, Femi turns **shame** at doing nothing into a plan.
He wants **company apprenticeships**, fitting his traditional views.
Both he and Ruth would be **retraining at once**.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding in the church hall as planned
Line up a plumbing apprenticeship to start in year two
Save part of every pay for the first time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and a man should be able to sort himself out in that time. I'd still want the company to train people, not just let them go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd breathe easier. Robots underground around 2039 means I'd be 40. Ten years is long enough for a man to learn a new trade, even a stubborn one like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling for a few years, have the wedding, maybe even a first child. I'd save, then start a plumbing apprenticeship at 30 or so. I'd keep going to church and stay close to the men there, because that's where the work comes from round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Still worried about the nickel price, but not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, God willing, in a couple of years. Ten years gives me time to get a trade before they're in school. I wouldn't feel that in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nickel price. A closure next year would hurt more than any robot ten years away. We've got two weeks of savings, so it doesn't take much.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty for a man to sort himself out.
I'd want the company to **train people**, not just let them go.
think: Robots arrive around **2039**, when I'm 40, so I have time.
Even a stubborn man can learn **a new trade** in ten years.
A **nickel price** crash could hit long before robots.
do: Keep **drilling** for a few years and marry Ruth.
Stay close to **church** contacts for work leads.
feel: Mostly **okay**, still worried about nickel prices.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a man to learn a new trade, even a stubborn one like me.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Femi plan **children** and a trade together.
The **nickel price** remains his nearest threat.
Church is his **job network**, not just faith.

steps.text: Keep drilling at Hollow Creek for a few more years
Marry Ruth and plan a first child
Start a plumbing apprenticeship around age 30

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Ruth and I would both lose our jobs within a few years, right when we're starting out. What would help is real apprenticeships, run by companies, paid properly, for men and women who've already been working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. I don't want a government cheque, I want a job, and if the robots take the job then somebody had better have a trade ready for me.

headlineQuote: I don't want a government cheque, I want a job, and if the robots take the job then somebody had better have a trade ready for me.
portrait: Femi, 27, runs a **jumbo drill** underground at Hollow Creek nickel mine, like his father and grandfather.
He's marrying Ruth, a **bank worker**, next autumn and has about two weeks of savings.
He distrusts AI and **city decision-makers** and prefers family and church to government help.
He's anxious in mild pictures and **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two or five years.
His steady fallback is a **plumbing apprenticeship**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with his and Ruth's jobs going **just as they marry**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid company apprenticeships** for people who've already been working.
